definition: Piecemeal means done gradually in small, disconnected pieces — one fragment at a time, with no overall plan coordinating the parts.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word piecemeal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know piecemeal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The museum assembled the dinosaur skeleton piecemeal, one donated crate of bones at a time, across thirty scattered years.
Gradual is weaker than piecemeal: gradual only says the change comes slowly, while piecemeal adds that it comes in disconnected scraps, with no plan holding the pieces together.
Haphazard goes further than piecemeal: piecemeal work still answers real needs one piece at a time, but haphazard work has lost order altogether — nothing decides what happens next.

Incremental means advancing by small planned steps, each building on the last — incremental change follows a design. Piecemeal shares the small steps but drops the design: the pieces arrive as chance allows, with no plan tying them together.

Fragmentary describes the state of a thing — existing in disconnected pieces, like a fragmentary manuscript. Piecemeal describes the process: work done one scrap at a time, so a piecemeal effort is what leaves a fragmentary result behind.

The meal you eat began as Old English mæl, 'a fixed time or measure' — the same word hiding at the end of piecemeal, where it still means 'one measure at a time.'

Ana and Luis furnished their first apartment piecemeal.
A kitchen table came from a March yard sale, two mismatched chairs from a cousin in June, a lamp rescued from a curb in October, a bookshelf the following spring.
Three years in, no two pieces matched and two rooms still stood half empty — there had never been a plan, only whatever turned up, whenever it happened to turn up.
The furnishing arrived one stray piece at a time, with no design tying the pieces together — change in unplanned fragments over years, which is exactly what piecemeal describes.

The opera house in Marlow burned in 1962, and the town never voted a restoration budget.
What repair happened, happened piecemeal.
A roofing company donated shingles one summer.
A decade later, a retired electrician rewired the lobby because he hated seeing it dark.
The balcony rail came from a demolished church two counties away.
No two jobs were coordinated.
Workers matched nothing to a master drawing, because there was none; each crew solved the problem in front of it and left.
Visitors today can read the whole history in the walls: six shades of brick, four styles of molding, wiring that loops around plaster nobody dared open.
Architecture students still visit, not to admire the craft but to see what forty years of uncoordinated repair leaves behind.
